title: Universal computation by braiding non-Abelian anyons

concept.text: The innovation would be a physical computing platform that stores quantum information collectively in non-Abelian anyons and performs universal quantum computation through protected braiding operations. Anyons are excitations whose exchanges can transform a quantum state. For non-Abelian anyons, the order of exchanges matters: exchanging particles in one sequence can produce a different operation from exchanging them in another sequence. Information is encoded in their fusion space—the possible collective quantum states associated with how the anyons can combine—rather than in a separately readable state of each particle.

The target combines a gapped computational bulk with the ability to create and initialize anyons, braid them, fuse them and read out their collective state. Universality means that compositions of the available operations can approximate arbitrary quantum computations to a chosen accuracy. Fibonacci anyon theory supplies a theoretical example of universality by braiding. Standard Majorana/Ising braiding has a more restricted computational repertoire and needs supplementary operations for universality; identifying Majorana-like states or measuring their parity would establish only part of the target.

significance.text: If realized with demonstrated protection, this would make the physical medium itself resist specified local disturbances during both information storage and native gate operations. Ideally, an operation depends on the topology of the braid rather than every microscopic detail of the particles’ paths. The direct advance would therefore be an encoding and gate mechanism with built-in physical protection, potentially reducing the burden of correcting the residual errors that remain.

The protection has specific operating conditions. Thermal creation of unwanted excitations can be exponentially suppressed when the energy gap is large relative to thermal energy. Effects arising from finite separation of the anyons can decrease exponentially as separation grows relative to a characteristic localization length. Neither statement is a general law for total gate error. Local disturbances can couple existing low-energy modes without creating new excitations across the bulk gap, while disorder-trapped quasiparticles, non-equilibrium poisoning, unintended braids, control mistakes and readout errors can still damage a computation.

Physical protection and active quantum error correction are compatible. A topological device could still require repeated measurements, decoding and correction to support long computations. Conversely, a successful actively corrected quantum computer would not by itself demonstrate universal computation by braiding. The supplied parity-readout paper explicitly discusses error-correction schemes that use topologically protected operations, illustrating how these mechanisms could work together.

Conditional downstream possibility: sufficiently reliable universal braiding could enable a scalable architecture for quantum algorithms while reducing some hardware or correction demands. That benefit would depend on initialization, readout, operation speed, fabrication, connectivity and residual-error management. Demonstrating topological protection alone would not establish useful computational scale, an advantageous total resource cost or a practical speedup.

missing_breakthrough.text: The capability to establish is an integrated physical system with a gapped computational bulk and controllable non-Abelian excitations whose protected operations are both composable and universal. A bulk gap can coexist with gapless edges, so evidence about an edge must be interpreted in relation to the actual computational degrees of freedom. The supplied evidence defines this target and documents partial results, but does not establish whether the complete capability remains undemonstrated across the field as of 1 November 2026.

A central barrier is distinguishing the intended topological states from alternatives that produce similar measurements. In semiconductor–superconductor devices, low-energy Andreev bound states can mimic aspects of Majorana-related parity signals. A convincing platform must connect evidence for the relevant phase and excitations to controlled fusion and braiding behavior. Parity readout is a necessary experimental capability for some architectures, but it does not by itself establish topological states or their computational operations.

Protection must also survive actual operation. Engineering barriers include maintaining sufficiently low temperature, controlling unwanted quasiparticles and poisoning, separating computational modes enough to limit their coupling, managing disorder and executing intended operations without introducing competing errors. Raising the gap or increasing separation does not automatically improve every contribution to logical error; the relevant error mechanism and operating regime must be identified and measured.

Universality is a separate barrier from demonstrating non-Abelian behavior. Standard Ising-type braids do not supply a universal gate set, including in the ν=5/2 setting discussed in the theoretical review. Adding an unprotected operation can make an architecture computationally universal while leaving the stronger goal of universal protected operations incomplete. A protected non-Clifford resource would help meet that goal only when combined with the other protected operations needed for universality.

current_state.text: The 2008 review by Nayak, Simon, Stern, Freedman and Das Sarma establishes the theoretical framework for non-Abelian fusion spaces, braid operations and topological quantum computation. It identifies Fibonacci anyon theory as a route to universality and explains the limitations of standard Ising-type braiding. These are theoretical foundations, not evidence that a universal physical device has been built. The supplied review examined a truncated extraction containing explicit statements supporting these distinctions; the detailed Fibonacci section was outside the retained excerpt.

On 19 February 2025, Microsoft Azure Quantum, M. Aghaee and collaborators published “Interferometric single-shot parity measurement in InAs–Al hybrid devices” in Nature, volume 638, pages 651–655. The reported achievement is single-shot fermion-parity readout, not a demonstrated computational braid. The article explicitly leaves open whether the measured low-energy states are topological and does not unequivocally distinguish Majorana zero modes from suitably tuned low-energy Andreev bound states.

That paper reports an assignment error probability of approximately 1% under optimal measurement conditions. The supplied review records that its supplement obtains an optimal measurement time of 32.5 microseconds using the measured signal-to-noise ratio and an assumed quasiparticle-poisoning time of 2 milliseconds. The 1% figure therefore concerns parity assignment under those conditions; it is not a demonstrated braid-gate error or a universal logical-computation error rate. The review had full article text and a partially retained supplement, but did not independently inspect the figures or raw data.

Henry F. Legg’s “On the robustness of topological gap detection via transport,” published on 24 June 2026 in Nature, volume 654, pages E22–E26, challenges the gap interpretation associated with the parity-readout work. Its accessible preview describes the relevant transport regions as substantially disordered and apparently gapless. The supplied review also examined correspondence containing Microsoft’s rebuttal that the parity measurements exclude a gapless regime, alongside disagreement about whether that rebuttal is conclusive. The full Legg article was behind subscription access. This record supports reporting a scientific dispute, not resolving the device’s gap structure.

The research additionally names an asserted preprint, “Observation of Time-Domain Braiding of Non-Abelian Anyons at ν=5/2,” identified as arXiv:2608.12897 and reportedly posted on 13 August 2026, with a claimed noise signature in a fractional-quantum-Hall edge. No saved artifact or source URL for that item is supplied, so its identity, posting date and reported findings remain unverified here; its full text was not reviewed. This limitation is not evidence that the item or result is false. Even if the described noise signature were confirmed, that observation alone would not establish protected, composable universal computational braiding.

Evidence scope: the supplied material supports the dated theoretical and experimental distinctions above, but contains no completed freshness assessment establishing field-wide coverage through 1 November 2026. It therefore supports neither a claim that the entire innovation has been achieved nor a definitive claim that every route to it remains experimentally unfulfilled.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: in one integrated device, establish a gapped computational bulk, reproducible initialization and fusion outcomes, and controlled braid operations acting on the encoded fusion space. Characterize enough operations and order-dependent compositions to test a non-Abelian braid representation. A single operation matching one predicted unitary, or a parity signal also compatible with trivial Andreev states, would not adequately distinguish the intended capability. These proposed criteria draw on the theoretical computational requirements and the documented limits of parity readout; they are not an established consensus certification protocol.
completion_criteria.label: Gapped device's order-dependent fusion-space braids test non-Abelian representation

completion_criteria.text: Proposed universality test: connect the measured elementary operations to a theoretically universal gate construction and demonstrate their composition on encoded states. A route using a protected non-Clifford resource must also demonstrate the other protected operations and consumption procedures required to make it computationally universal. Tests should include representative sequences of increasing complexity, with predictions and uncertainty estimates that distinguish the intended operations from plausible alternatives. Finite experiments establish the demonstrated breadth and consistency of this construction; they cannot test every possible quantum computation.
completion_criteria.label: Increasingly complex encoded compositions match a universal gate construction

completion_criteria.text: Proposed protection test: under controlled temperature, timing and noise conditions, show that the relevant logical-error contributions decrease as the gap relative to thermal energy or the anyon separation relative to the localization length increases. Separate thermal excitation, finite-separation coupling, poisoning, control and readout contributions where feasible. The objective is to demonstrate the claimed protection mechanism within a measured regime, rather than require total error to decrease monotonically with either parameter regardless of other changes.
completion_criteria.label: Logical-error contributions fall with gap-to-thermal-energy or separation-to-localization ratio

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: repeat the fusion, braid, composition and protection measurements across preparations and devices, provide sufficient methods and data for independent replication, and report operating windows, device variability, computation duration and failure rates. Characterize the remaining need for active correction, as well as initialization, readout and throughput limits. Such demonstrations would establish a concrete experimental capability within stated boundaries, without automatically establishing scalable manufacturing, commercially useful performance or arbitrary computational size.
completion_criteria.label: Replicated measurements with methods, data and stated practical limits

related_concepts.text: Roster comparison—QUA-01, “Distance-scalable universal fault-tolerant quantum computation”: QUA-05 concerns the physical encoding and protected operations supplied by non-Abelian anyons. QUA-01 concerns universal fault tolerance that improves with increasing code distance. These capabilities could coexist in one machine: topological hardware may still use active correction. Universal braiding alone would not establish distance scaling, and distance-scalable fault tolerance could use a different physical platform. This comparison follows the supplied roster title rather than a full QUA-01 specification.

Roster synthesis—QUA-04, “A laboratory material that stores a logical qubit passively at nonzero temperature,” and QUA-08, “Local, universal fault tolerance whose overhead stays bounded as the error falls”: QUA-04 shares the ambition of physical protection but centers on passive storage at nonzero temperature. QUA-05 additionally requires controlled universal computation and does not establish passive memory stability merely by having a bulk gap. QUA-08 concerns locality and asymptotic overhead; successful anyon braiding would still need separate evidence for those properties.

Roster synthesis—QUA-06, “Fault-tolerant quantum interconnects that let processors scale by adding modules,” and QUA-10, “Foundry-made fault-tolerant quantum computation without a dilution refrigerator”: QUA-06 addresses protected communication and modular scaling, which universal braiding inside a device would not automatically provide. QUA-10 adds fabrication and refrigeration requirements that are independent of the braid-based computational principle. A QUA-05 platform could eventually contribute to either architecture, but its achievement would not satisfy those entries by itself.

Roster synthesis—QUA-02, “Cryptographically relevant execution of Shor’s algorithm,” QUA-03, “Experimentally confirmed quantum prediction of sign-problematic matter,” and QUA-09, “An end-to-end superpolynomial quantum speedup on large classical data”: these are application or performance outcomes that a sufficiently capable QUA-05 machine might support. Universal protected operations would not alone demonstrate cryptographic scale, experimentally validated predictions of difficult matter, or an end-to-end speedup after accounting for classical-data handling and other costs.

Roster synthesis—QUA-07, “A proof that quantum polynomial time exceeds classical polynomial time on decision problems”: this is a mathematical complexity separation. A universal braid-based computer would realize a physical model of quantum computation, but would not itself prove that separation. The entries address distinct achievements and remain separate.

brief.title: Quantum computing with physically protected operations
possible: People could run quantum computations with information protected by the material that holds it. The information would live in the shared states of anyons: particle-like disturbances in a material. Exchanging them along interwoven paths, called braiding, would perform calculations.

The order of those exchanges would change the result. Combined braids would approximate any quantum computation to a chosen accuracy, while protecting both stored information and computing operations from local disturbances.
why: For quantum computer builders, this would put some protection against errors directly into the hardware. Operations would depend on how the paths intertwine, rather than every detail of their shape. That could reduce the work needed to correct errors during a calculation.

sources.who: Chetan Nayak, Steven H. Simon, Ady Stern, Michael Freedman and Sankar Das Sarma
sources.showed: Their review explains how shared particle states and braiding could support protected quantum computing. It describes a theoretical route to arbitrary computations and explains why some kinds of anyons have a more limited repertoire.
sources.cited_for: The theory connects collective information storage, braiding and physical protection.
sources.not_established: The theoretical framework does not demonstrate a working physical computer.

sources.who: Microsoft Azure Quantum, Morteza Aghaee and collaborators
sources.showed: They measured parity, which distinguishes an even from an odd particle count, in a semiconductor–superconductor device. The reported assignment error was about 1% under optimal conditions.
sources.quote: We achieve an assignment error probability of 1% for optimal measurement time.
sources.cited_for: The experiment demonstrates a readout capability needed by some proposed computing architectures.
sources.not_established: The measurement does not distinguish the intended protected states from alternatives or demonstrate computational braiding.

sources.showed: His analysis of electrical transport data found considerable disorder and apparently no energy gap in the operating regions used for Microsoft's parity measurements. Microsoft disputes that interpretation.
sources.quote: and this analysis reveals that the claimed parity readout occurred in regions of phase space with considerable disorder that appear gapless.
sources.cited_for: The analysis challenges whether the device has the energy barrier required for the proposed protection.
sources.not_established: The dispute leaves the device's energy gap unresolved and does not settle whether protected computing operations are possible.

shown: Nayak and colleagues describe a theoretical route to universal computing by braiding. Microsoft's experimental advance is a measurement of parity in a semiconductor–superconductor device.
missing: An integrated device must connect the intended anyons to reproducible preparation, combination, braiding and readout.
Protected operations must combine into a set capable of approximating arbitrary quantum computations.
Measured computing errors must demonstrate the claimed physical protection during operation.
Repeated results across devices must establish reliability and practical operating limits.

milestones.label: A device demonstrates exchanges whose order changes the result
milestones.explanation: A device would need an energy barrier to bulk excitations, reproducible anyon preparation and combination, and order-dependent braids acting on shared states. Together, these would test the intended particle behavior.

milestones.label: Longer sequences follow a universal computing construction
milestones.explanation: Measured protected operations would have to match a theoretical construction for arbitrary quantum computations through increasingly complex sequences. This would test whether the operations combine as required.

milestones.label: Relevant errors fall as physical protection increases
milestones.explanation: Under controlled conditions, relevant error contributions would have to fall as the energy barrier grows relative to heat, or separation grows relative to particle spread. This would test the claimed protection mechanism.

milestones.label: Repeated experiments establish reliability and practical limits
milestones.explanation: Preparation, combination, braiding, composition and protection results would have to repeat across devices, with methods and data enabling independent replication. Operating and correction limits would define the demonstrated capability.

uncertain: Whether Microsoft's device has the energy gap needed for protection remains disputed.
The statistical tests and practical performance thresholds for judging completion remain to be specified.
Physical protection may still need active error correction; its overall resource advantage remains open.

page.title: Universal quantum computation by braiding non-Abelian anyons
page.definition: A gapped physical system stores quantum information in the shared fusion states of non-Abelian anyons, excitations whose exchanges act in an order-dependent way. Braiding supplies gates that approximate arbitrary quantum circuits, with storage and gates protected against local perturbations by the topological phase.

goal.need: Error correction can require many physical qubits for one encoded qubit: Google's distance-7 surface-code memory used 101 physical qubits and had a logical error probability of 0.143% ± 0.003% per correction cycle. Non-Abelian anyons offer a different encoding in which local perturbations are suppressed by the physical phase, and braiding performs gates on that encoding.

statements.body: US Department of Energy, Office of Science
statements.quote: Braiding can thus be applied to perform logical gate operations on a quantum bit, or qubit.
statements.context: The associated experiment concerns Abelian quantum Hall anyons; this passage motivates the broader anyon-computing programme.

statements.quote: Non-Abelian anyons could open a new avenue for quantum computation
statements.context: The statement accompanies a programmable-processor demonstration of projective Ising anyons, whose braids alone are not computationally universal.

completion.title: An integrated physical device performs universal computation with topologically protected anyon braids.
completion.criterion: Demonstrate initialization, computational braiding and readout in one gapped physical system of non-Abelian anyons. Establish that its braid generators realize a representation whose compositions approximate arbitrary encoded quantum circuits to any prescribed accuracy, including entangling operations. Demonstrate the encoding's protection against local perturbations during storage and gates. Universality must arise from braid operations, including in a digitally realized platform.
completion.set_by: Atlas synthesis of published physical requirements and mathematical universality criteria; no external integrated hardware acceptance test was found.
completion.basis: Searches of NIST and ISO material, DARPA targets, Microsoft roadmaps and experimental anyon papers found no integrated hardware acceptance test or common fidelity cutoff. This synthesis combines physical topological protection with mathematical braid universality. The 2026 S3 experiment obtains universality using fusion as an additional primitive, so it does not establish universality of braids alone.

milestones.title: Non-Abelian anyon pairs are created and their fusion rules are verified.
milestones.criterion: Create anyon pairs, control which pairs are fused, and measure the resulting collective charges against the proposed non-Abelian fusion rules. Google reported creation and fusion of projective Ising defects on a 25-qubit processor on 11 May 2023. The superconductor-hybrid paper published on 19 February 2025 studied two InAs–Al devices and reported 1% parity-assignment error under optimal conditions. Its authors state that the measurement does not determine whether the detected states are topological. Parity readout alone does not establish this milestone.
milestones.set_by: Google Quantum AI and Collaborators, published experimental requirements (1) and (2) in Non-Abelian braiding of graph vertices in a superconducting processor.
milestones.threshold_quote: verify the rules that govern the ‘collision’ of two anyons, known as the fusion rules

milestones.title: An anyon encoding suppresses locally induced splitting and dephasing exponentially.
milestones.criterion: Establish that local perturbations cannot resolve the encoded degeneracy except for the predicted finite-size corrections. The published Majorana protocol tests correlated scaling of the splitting frequency ω0 and dephasing rate 1/T2: both must fall exponentially with a protection parameter. For its 1/f-noise, overlap-dominated model, ω0 ∼ 1/T2 ∼ exp(−L/ξ), where L is mode separation and ξ is localization length; other noise models change the relation. The cited parity-readout result does not measure these linked scalings.
milestones.set_by: Local protection is a field requirement reviewed by Nayak et al.; the explicit linked-scaling protocol is Aasen et al., Section IV, written for Majorana nanowires.
milestones.threshold_quote: must scale with one another, and they must both scale exponentially with some parameter.

milestones.title: Braiding realizes noncommuting transformations of an anyon-encoded state.
milestones.criterion: Execute braid operators A and B for which AB and BA act differently on the encoded fusion space. Aasen's Majorana protocol tests one generator using one braid (readout probabilities 1/2, 1/2), two braids (a certain flip in the ideal limit), and a no-braid control. For quantum Hall fluids, Alkalay et al.'s preprint of 13 August 2026 reports edge partition-noise signatures consistent with time-domain braiding at filling ν = 5/2. That result is not peer reviewed and does not implement an encoded computational gate.
milestones.set_by: The field definition of non-Abelian statistics in Nayak et al., Section II.1.1; the specified Majorana control experiments are Aasen et al., Section V.
milestones.threshold_quote: Unless they commute for any interchange of particles, in which case the particles’ braiding statistics is Abelian

milestones.title: Braids approximate arbitrary single-qubit rotations.
milestones.criterion: Realize elementary braids whose representation on one encoded qubit is dense in SU(2), up to overall phase, so sequences approximate any single-qubit rotation. A mathematical density result must be connected to the implemented anyon operations; finitely many measured rotations alone do not prove density. Xu et al.'s report of 29 March 2024, subsequently published in Nature Physics, created two pairs of Fibonacci excitations on 27 transmon qubits and implemented braiding sequences supporting universal single-qubit gates through digital quantum simulation.
milestones.set_by: The field's single-qubit universality criterion, stated for Fibonacci encodings by Carnahan, Zeuch and Bonesteel, Section I.
milestones.threshold_quote: Braids which approximate any desired single-qubit gate

milestones.title: Braiding implements an entangling gate on two anyon-encoded computational units.
milestones.criterion: Implement an entangling braid between two encoded computational units, using an encoding compatible with single-unit gates. For Fibonacci qubits, the published constructions also suppress leakage out of the computational subspace as the braid is refined. As partial results in programmable arrays, Google entangled three logical qubits encoded in eight defects in 2023. Lo et al., published on 15 July 2026, prepared a 54-qubit S3 ground state and implemented entangling braids; universality in that experiment additionally uses fusion. Neither result establishes a protected universal braid-only processor.
milestones.set_by: The field's entangling-gate requirement; Carnahan, Zeuch and Bonesteel publish constructions specifically for Fibonacci qubits.
milestones.threshold_quote: to systematically construct entangling gates for two qubits encoded by Fibonacci anyons.
